item.title: Panel Local Projections with Missing Data
item.description: arXiv:2611.10372v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A panel local projection can remain identified even when missing data leave no complete regression case. We recover the projection over specified dates by combining factor-based conditional means with idiosyncratic covariances from observed pairs. Under strong factors in the auxiliary panel, sufficient factor variation at observed dates and enough observations of the required pairs, a second-order expansion yields bias-corrected moments and a joint score for inference. The localized multiplier bootstrap provides pointwise confidence intervals and simultaneous bands under additional dependence restrictions. We revisit the investment response to geopolitical risk studied by Caldara and Iacoviello (2022) with a larger quarterly firm sample and extend the analysis to monthly projections of trailing-three-month investment intensity. In the monthly analysis, the six-month response difference between high- and low-exposure firms becomes more negative as firms with incomplete histories enter the sample.
item.dc:creator: Yubo Tao

item.title: Asymptotic Theory of Integrated Pairwise-Difference Functionals of Kernel Estimators, with Applications to Treatment Effect Heterogeneity
item.description: arXiv:2611.10383v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper develops asymptotic theory for integrated pairwise-difference statistics constructed from kernel estimators, with applications to treatment effect heterogeneity. The statistics integrate absolute or positive-part differences between kernel estimates evaluated at pairs of points. Their two-point structure falls outside existing one-point $L_1$-type functional theory. We establish asymptotic normality using a H\'ajek-type projection of a Poissonized statistic and develop feasible centering and variance estimators. We consider two applications. First, we test whether treatment effects vary with one covariate block while holding another fixed. Second, we establish root-$N$ inference for the directional Gini mean difference of the conditional treatment effect function, which measures heterogeneity in outcome units. The framework also accommodates tests of monotone effect modification and estimated pseudo-outcomes. Simulations corroborate the asymptotic theory and show good finite-sample performance. An application to 401(k) eligibility and net financial assets illustrates the usefulness of the proposed tests.
item.dc:creator: Julius Owusu

item.title: Good Looks and the Academic Job Market: Measuring Attractiveness with Vision Embeddings
item.description: arXiv:2611.10447v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a new approach to measure physical attractiveness---the relative vision embedding (RVE) score. The score maps a face to a vector in the embedding space of a pre-trained deep vision model and measures its proximity to a reference set of celebrity faces. It requires no additional training or fine-tuning, no hand-crafted features, and no human raters; it is continuous, inexpensive, scalable, and fully reproducible. Using publicly available photographs with human attractiveness ratings, we show that the RVE scores correlate strongly with human ratings and that rankings are consistent across several off-the-shelf vision models. We apply the measure to administrative hiring data from a research-oriented economics department, complemented by hand-collected photographs of the job applicants. Higher RVE scores are associated with better job-market outcomes, though the association is not robust across all specifications. In contrast, the association with reference-letter length and sentiment is strong and robust: candidates with higher RVE scores receive longer letters written in more favorable language, and this sentiment gradient is steeper for female candidates. The pattern is consistent with appearance affecting academic hiring in part through letters of recommendation.
item.dc:creator: Fabian Slonimczyk, Shergazy Kimsanbaev

item.title: Z-Estimation under Unignorably Large Clusters
item.description: arXiv:2611.10925v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cluster-size heterogeneity can invalidate conventional cluster-robust inference when a small number of clusters dominate observation-weighted estimating equations. This paper develops asymptotic theory for cluster-balanced \(Z\)-estimators under independent clusters, arbitrary realised cluster sizes, and unrestricted within-cluster dependence. Building on the size-adjusted reweighting of Chiang, Sasaki & Wang (2025), the analysis distinguishes target definition, identification, and inference. A common cluster-level zero, imposed as an identifying condition or derived from individual-level exogeneity or design-based mechanisms, makes the structural target invariant to deterministic cluster reweighting; separation of the reweighted population moments then ensures identification. The pointwise results establish asymptotic normality while allowing the covariance sequence to vary along the cluster array. The results for functional parameters establish weak convergence and validity of a cluster multiplier bootstrap for uniform inference. The framework covers smooth and non-smooth scores with distribution, quantile, and expectile regressions as concrete applications. Monte Carlo experiments illustrate pointwise and uniform inference under heterogeneous cluster sizes, and a supplementary empirical application illustrates the consequences of cluster weighting in municipal-school data.
item.dc:creator: Agossou Michel Yomakou, Abderrahim Taamouti, Emmanuel S. Tsyawo

item.title: Do Modern Difference-in-Differences Estimators Change Published Findings in Business Research?
item.description: arXiv:2611.11003v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Staggered-adoption difference-in-differences (DiD) designs are a workhorse of empirical research in business-school journals. The two-way fixed effects (TWFE) estimator that typically implements them can place negative weights on heterogeneous treatment effects. We ask whether negative weights change published findings by reanalyzing staggered-adoption specifications in business-school journals with journal-wide public replication archives. Following Hull (2026), we use large language model agents to identify eligible specifications, replicate the published TWFE estimate, and re-estimate each specification with the DiD-averaging estimator of Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021) and the imputation estimator of Borusyak et al. (2024). We re-estimate 355 specifications from 40 papers. Across the 283 DiD-averaging and 306 imputation comparisons that pass Hull's leverage screen, from 28 and 29 papers, TWFE and modern estimates have correlations of 0.61 and 0.70, change sign in 25.1 and 18.0 percent of comparisons, and differ significantly with opposite signs in 10.2 and 7.2 percent. Modern standard errors are 1.61 and 1.30 times those of TWFE. Including the comparisons that fail the screen leaves these figures essentially unchanged. Our results suggest that TWFE and heterogeneity-robust estimators disagree in a non-negligible share of the published staggered designs we re-estimate, and more often than in economics.
item.dc:creator: Davide Proserpio

item.title: Testing Conditional Moment Restrictions in Networks
item.description: arXiv:2611.11183v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Parametric models of network formation, such as dyadic logit models, are increasingly popular, but few tools exist to test their specification. This paper develops a specification test for conditionally independent dyad (CID) models based on the probabilities that these models assign to subgraphs, the patterns of links among small groups of agents. Given the agents' characteristics, a parametric CID model determines not only the probability of each link but also the probability that a group of agents forms a triangle, a star, or any other subgraph. Under correct specification, the expected frequency of each subgraph among agents with given characteristics equals its model-implied probability. This forms the basis of the testable conditional moment restrictions. The test statistic is the weighted integrated squared distance between a nonparametric kernel estimate of these probabilities and the probabilities implied by the estimated parametric model. I derive its asymptotic distribution under the null hypothesis.
item.dc:creator: Wenxuan Ding

item.title: When the Norm is Wrong: Social Norm Misspecification and Targeting with an Application to Microfinance Adoption
item.description: arXiv:2611.12255v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Structural models of peer effects typically capture peer influence through the average, aggregate, or in some cases through extreme peer actions. Such specifications, however, are imposed ex ante and are typically ad hoc. We study the consequences of social norm misspecification by extending the constant elasticity of substitution (CES) norm from continuous to discrete choices. Considering a binary-choice game with incomplete information, we derive results on existence and uniqueness of a rational expectations equilibrium and establish conditions for identification of the structural parameters. We estimate the model by the Nested Pseudo-Likelihood estimator, implemented using the spectral algorithm. Monte Carlo simulations show that the CES estimates of the peer effects approach their true values as the sample grows, whereas imposing a linear norm biases them even in large samples. We apply the framework to microfinance adoption in India and find a strongly max-leaning norm, with significant heterogeneity in curvature and peer effects across villages grouped by caste composition and wealth. In a counterfactual exercise that allocates a fixed subsidy budget to maximise adoption, the estimated and linear norms target very different households, with the former favouring village "leaders", who are more likely to adopt and were the first to be informed about microfinance.
item.dc:creator: Shantanu Chadha

item.title: Weak-Instrument Inference and Model Diagnostics in Double Machine Learning for Linear Instrumental Variable Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.10863v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study weak-instrument-robust inference in partially linear instrumental-variables models with learned nuisances. Building on an i.i.d. uniform-size baseline, we establish uniform asymptotic validity of clustered cross-fitted Anderson-Rubin inference and cross-fitted score inference under the stated sampling and nuisance-rate conditions. Extensions establish Anderson-Rubin validity for survey-weighted target laws and fold-nested generated instruments. A supporting population benchmark shows that prediction-optimal instrument residualization maximizes concentration when the treatment nuisance is correctly specified. A five-design diagnostic portfolio, a known-truth Monte Carlo, and an exploratory selector examine how nuisance specification and estimation affect realized strength and inference.
item.dc:creator: Airui Meng

item.title: Polynomial-Preserving Processes and Volatility Modelling in Discrete Time
item.description: arXiv:2611.10928v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper develops a discrete-time framework for volatility modelling and derivative pricing based on polynomial preservation. The framework provides exact moments of arbitrary order and serial cross-moments of variance and return processes over any finite horizon through finite-dimensional matrix representations. This analytical tractability is maintained while accommodating flexible leverage and variance-of-variance dynamics and non-Gaussian innovations. We introduce two novel classes of stochastic volatility models that nest widely used discrete-time specifications and study their statistical properties. Under two distinct scaling regimes, we establish weak convergence to polynomial diffusions and jump-diffusions and convergence of polynomial moments, linking discrete-time moment recursions to continuous-time matrix-exponential formulas. An empirical analysis of S\&P~500 returns and a large panel of options spanning 1996--2023 shows that the proposed specifications improve return fit and reduce mean weekly implied volatility root mean squared errors by approximately 8--41\% relative to their nested benchmarks, depending on the variance dynamics and innovation distribution.
item.dc:creator: Maciej Augustyniak, Alexandru Badescu, Zekun Zhang

item.title: Bayesian precision factor models for high-dimensional macroeconomic time series
item.description: arXiv:2611.12368v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Series in a macroeconomic panel are almost all correlated with one another, which makes correlation a poor guide to which pairs are directly linked. For example, Treasury rates at different maturities are all highly correlated, yet a short and a long rate may be related only through the rates at maturities between them; similarly, sectors of the economy such as output, employment, prices, and interest rates may be related directly or only through other series. Both are questions about the inverse covariance matrix. Recovering it from quarterly data is difficult: contemporaneous dependence is entangled with temporal dynamics, the innovations remain densely dependent once those dynamics are removed, and the number of series is comparable to the number of quarters observed. We propose VAPOR (Vector Autoregressive Precision factOR), a Bayesian model that estimates vector autoregressive dynamics jointly with a factor-structured innovation precision matrix, inferring the partial correlations directly from the fitted precision rather than imposing a zero pattern. Applied to 100 quarterly FRED-QD series, VAPOR learns from the data that each Treasury rate is directly related only to the rates at adjacent maturities, places all 26 selected dependencies within a single FRED-QD group, and attains the lowest held-out prediction error among the estimators compared.
item.dc:creator: Peter Dunson

item.title: Average versus expected causal effects under interference: Modeling assumptions and estimation bottlenecks
item.description: arXiv:2611.12690v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Causal inference under treatment interference requires assumptions to reduce the exponentially large number of potential outcomes. We develop hierarchical finite-population models for potential outcomes by separating these assumptions into three layers: interference neighborhoods, exposure mappings, and outcome models. Given an interference neighborhood and exposure mapping, we show that potential outcomes admit a nonparametric decomposition into direct, spillover, and treatment--spillover interaction components. This decomposition provides a common coordinate system for nonparametric, semiparametric, and parametric models of finite-population potential outcomes. For a given potential-outcome model, we define two classes of estimands. Average causal effects (ACEs), such as direct and total treatment effects, contrast potential outcomes under fixed treatment--exposure conditions. Expected causal effects (ECEs), such as expected direct and indirect effects, contrast expectations of potential outcomes under a specified allocation policy. For both classes, we bound the variance of the canonical Horvitz--Thompson estimator by three terms: a diagonal weight term, a term from overlapping interference neighborhoods, and a residual design-dependence term. Our upper and lower bounds show that under graph-unaware designs, nonparametric design-unbiased estimation of ACEs can require sample sizes growing exponentially in the interference degree, whereas polynomial growth can suffice for design-aligned ECEs. Under neighborhood interference, we construct graph-aware independent-set designs with variance bounds polynomial in the maximum degree for direct and total treatment effects on every graph, whereas graph cluster randomization can incur worst-case variance exponential in the degree.
item.dc:creator: Vishesh Karwa, Edoardo M. Airoldi, Donald B. Rubin

item.title: Tracking the economy at high frequency
item.description: arXiv:2507.07450v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper develops a high-frequency economic indicator using a Bayesian Dynamic Factor Model estimated with mixed-frequency data. The model incorporates weekly, monthly, and quarterly official indicators, and allows for dynamic heterogeneity and stochastic volatility. To ensure temporal consistency and avoid irregular aggregation artifacts, we introduce a pseudo-week structure that harmonizes the timing of observations. Our framework integrates dispersed and asynchronous official statistics into a unified High-Frequency Economic Index (HFEI), enabling real-time economic monitoring even in environments characterized by severe data limitations. We apply this framework to construct a high-frequency indicator for Ecuador, a country where official data are sparse and highly asynchronous, and compute pseudo-weekly recession probabilities using a time-varying mean regime-switching model fitted to the resulting index.
item.dc:creator: Yanina Baja\~na-Villag\'omez, Freddy Garc\'ia-Alb\'an, Juan Jarr\'in, Ramon Villa-Cox

item.title: Combining stated and revealed preferences: Matched and unmatched
item.description: arXiv:2507.13552v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Can stated preferences inform counterfactual analyses of actual choice? This research proposes a novel approach for researchers who have access to both stated choices in hypothetical scenarios and actual choices, matched or unmatched. The key idea is to use stated choices to control for individual unobserved heterogeneity. If this unobserved heterogeneity is the source of endogeneity, the researcher can correct for its influence in a choice function estimation using actual choices and recover causal effects. Bounds on causal effects are derived in the case where stated choices and actual choices are observed in unmatched data sets. These data combination bounds are of independent interest. We derive valid bootstrap inference for the bounds and show its good performance in a simulation experiment. We illustrate the method in an analysis of retirement decisions based on the Health and Retirement Study.
item.dc:creator: Romuald Meango, Marc Henry, Ismael Mourifie, Ju Hyun Oh

item.title: Semiparametric Identification of the Discount Factor and Payoff Function in Dynamic Discrete Choice Models
item.description: arXiv:2507.19814v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper studies the identification of the discount factor and payoff function in stationary infinite-horizon dynamic discrete choice models. In single-agent models, we show that nonparametric assumptions on per-period payoffs implied by economic theory, such as homogeneity, monotonicity, concavity, zero cross-differences, and complementarity, yield polynomial equalities and inequalities in the discount factor. These restrictions can identify the discount factor and the payoff function without normalizing the payoff of one action. Even when the payoff function is not point identified, they may still identify the discount factor. In dynamic games, we identify firm-specific discount factors by combining the irrelevance of other firms' lagged actions with restrictions such as exchangeability, even when the scrap value is unknown. We illustrate the approach with numerical examples and an empirical application to farmers' crop choices.
item.dc:creator: Yu Hao, Hiroyuki Kasahara, Katsumi Shimotsu

item.title: Debiased Kernel Estimation of Spot Volatility in the Presence of Infinite Variation Jumps
item.description: arXiv:2510.14285v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Volatility estimation is a central problem in financial econometrics, but becomes particularly challenging when jump activity is high, a phenomenon observed empirically in highly traded financial securities. In this paper, we revisit the problem of spot volatility estimation for an It\^o semimartingale with jumps of unbounded variation. We construct truncated kernel-based estimators and debiased variants that extend rate-optimal spot volatility estimation to a wider range of jump activity indices, from the previously available bound $Y<4/3$ to $Y<20/11$. Rate-suboptimal CLTs are also established for $Y>20/11$. Compared with earlier work, our approach achieves smaller asymptotic variances through the use of more general kernels and an optimal choice for the bandwidth convergence rate, and also has broader applicability under more flexible model assumptions. A comprehensive simulation study confirms that our procedures outperform competing methods in finite samples.
item.dc:creator: B. Cooper Boniece, Jos\'e E. Figueroa-L\'opez, Tianwei Zhou

item.title: Identification-aware Markov chain Monte Carlo
item.description: arXiv:2511.12847v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In Bayesian analysis, a proper posterior can exist even when identification fails, but its existence does not ensure reliable posterior computation. More broadly, posterior simulation can be slow when local samplers must move between separated regions or along ridges and weakly curved directions. We develop identification-aware Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) samplers that combine local updates with moves across observationally equivalent parameter values, thereby giving identification analysis a constructive role in modern Bayesian analysis. Under uniform mixing and communication conditions, we establish spectral-gap comparisons in which local-sampler upper bounds vanish as modes separate or likelihood-flat fibers expand, while lower bounds for identification-aware samplers remain bounded away from zero. Simulations illustrate these mechanisms. Structural vector moving-average (SVMA) applications at two scales demonstrate substantial sampling improvements under weak priors, with limited additional gains under strong priors.
item.dc:creator: Toru Kitagawa, Yizhou Kuang

item.title: Double Machine Learning for Inequality Decompositions: Reference Outcomes, Orthogonal Scores and Limited Overlap
item.description: arXiv:2511.13433v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Kitagawa-Oaxaca-Blinder decompositions split a gap in mean outcomes between two groups into a part explained by characteristics and an unexplained part. The unexplained part depends on the counterfactual "reference outcome" that individuals would receive if characteristics were valued equally. Several competing references have been proposed, mostly within the linear regression model. We show that the main proposals, namely using the outcome of either group as the reference and the references of Cotton (1988), Reimers (1983) and Neumark (1988), all belong to a single family of mixtures of the two groups' potential outcomes. This separates the choice of target from the choice of estimator, and allows nonparametric estimation by double machine learning. We find that the appropriate orthogonal score depends on the reference: Neumark's propensity-weighted reference requires a pooled regression, while all the others require group-specific regressions. We then show that Neumark's reference avoids both extrapolation and extreme weights under limited overlap. Finally, we discuss in a general setting the shrinkage effect of the unexplained part associated with the choice of Neumark's reference.
item.dc:creator: Emmanuel Flachaire, Bertille Picard

item.title: Difference-in-differences with a mediator
item.description: arXiv:2604.24049v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Causal mediation analysis is a powerful tool for decomposing the total effect of a treatment into its direct effect on the outcome and its indirect effect mediated through an intermediate variable. However, in observational studies, confounding between treatment and potential outcomes typically renders the total and natural effects non-identifiable. In this work, we advance the mediation analysis within the difference-in-differences framework. Under a mediator-adjusted parallel trends assumption and additional conditions, we demonstrate that natural indirect, direct, and total effects are identifiable in the treated group. We further derive efficient influence functions for these estimands, enabling the construction of multiply robust and nonparametrically efficient estimators. Applying our methodology to data from the Job Corps Study, we find that job training has a positive direct effect on short-term earnings, holding employment intensity fixed at its level under training, which is masked in the total effect by reduced work time; in the longer run, the total effect is positive and operates mainly through higher employment intensity.
item.dc:creator: Yuhao Deng, Haoyu Wei, Zhongzhe Ouyang

item.title: Learning Where to Look: Delaunay Matching for Discovery and Data Collection
item.description: arXiv:2607.04885v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A researcher observes a population in the status quo and wants to learn from a small, possibly selected sample exposed to an intervention its effect on the rest of the population. How should they combine these sources of information? And who should receive the intervention next to improve on estimation the most? I focus on convex matching estimators and answer both questions by adopting a statistical decision theoretic perspective and drawing new connections with results from computational geometry. First, I show that interpolation over the Delaunay simplex containing a target point minimizes worst-case bias. Second, I provide robust confidence intervals and show that inference-optimal weighting rules lay on a frontier that connects the proposed estimator to Synthetic Controls. Finally, I characterize the minimax refinement problem and show that the Delaunay triangulation of the existing data provides sufficient information to solve it numerically and restricts the space \textit{where to look} for optimal additions. In a semi-synthetic application in development economics, I show that Delaunay matching achieves a lower worst-case bias compared to commonly used estimators in practice (e.g. around 7 times smaller than synthetic controls) and that the minimax collection plan decreases it by around 90% within 20 additions.
item.dc:creator: Giacomo Opocher

item.title: Specification Testing for Dyadic Regression Models
item.description: arXiv:2607.26366v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Of the 88 empirical papers on dyadic or other relational data that we reviewed in the top five economics journals, 55 (62.5\%) use a linear specification. To assess whether such a specification describes the conditional mean, we develop Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Cram\'er-von Mises tests for undirected dyadic data that also accommodate smooth nonlinear specifications. To our knowledge, this paper is the first to develop omnibus specification tests for undirected dyadic regression models. A corrected first-order multiplier bootstrap is asymptotically exact in two standard Gaussian cases: the first-order nondegenerate case and independent dyads case. For a general class of such processes, we establish that a second-order multiplier bootstrap consistently approximates the limiting law uniformly over the indexing function class, even when the indexing functions are estimated. For the specification tests, we augment this bootstrap to account for two additional sources of non-Gaussianity: parameter estimation and the curvature of the regression function. We then construct an envelope test that is asymptotically exact in both Gaussian cases and controls size in the other degenerate cases. Simulations illustrate the size and power of the tests. In an application to housing sales, we reject a common mean price gap within distance bands but do not reject separate linear relationships by metro access.
item.dc:creator: Ulrich Hounyo, Jiahao Lin, Xiaojun Song

item.title: Choosing the Dictionary and Penalty for IV-LASSO
item.description: arXiv:2609.07033v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Estimating an instrumental variables (IV) first stage with the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) requires choosing a dictionary and penalty. Existing rules target first-stage objectives rather than precision of the structural parameter estimate. We derive a feasible approximate mean squared error (AMSE) criterion for full-sample IV-LASSO with one endogenous regressor and homoskedastic Gaussian errors. For a prespecified list of dictionary-penalty pairs, the criterion trades off approximation of the optimal instrument against a complexity cost that depends on the first two moments of the LASSO effective dimension and on the degree of endogeneity. The selected pair attains the smallest candidate-specific AMSE component up to vanishing relative error. In simulations calibrated to Paravisini et al. (2015), the criterion improves substantially on plug-in rules at low endogeneity and on cross-validation at high endogeneity, with nearly identical results under non-Gaussian errors. A supplementary appendix formally extends analysis to a class of non-Gaussian errors.
item.dc:creator: Yukun Ma, Manu Navjeevan, Bogdan Salahub

item.title: An Algebraic Approach to Continuously Updating GMM: Estimation and Inference
item.description: arXiv:2609.36445v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The continuously updating GMM estimator (CUE) minimizes a nonconvex objective. We give an algebraic solution in linear instrumental variables models with a fixed joint variance estimate that allows for heteroskedasticity, autocorrelation, or clustering. With one endogenous regressor and a positive definite variance estimate, the objective is a ratio of polynomials. Its global minimum is obtained by comparing the objective at no more than 4k-2 real stationary points and at infinity, with k instruments. The roots can be computed as eigenvalues of a companion matrix. We extend the results to singular variance estimates and characterize the multivariate minimum using finitely many stationary objective values. These results provide methods for computing CUE, overidentification statistics, and likelihood ratio-based tests. Simulations show that local optimization can lead to substantially different estimates and test decisions. The algebraic results are exact, although their numerical implementation requires care in computing polynomial coefficients and roots.
item.dc:creator: Marcelo J. Moreira, Whitney K. Newey, Mahrad Sharifvaghefi

item.title: Regret Equals Integrated Covariance: Exact Identities for the Value of Information in Stochastic Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2611.05227v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: For a stochastic program $\min_{z\in Z} c^T z + h(z)$ with a random cost vector $c$, regret, or the expected value of perfect information, is usually computed by re-solving the problem scenario by scenario. We show that regret is determined by the covariance between the cost vector and the optimal decision $\pi^s(c)$. The identity is exact and holds without regularity assumptions once the covariance is integrated along the path from the mean to each scenario. With $c_s=E[c]+s(c-E[c])$, $Reg=-\int_0^1 s^{-1} Cov(c_s,\pi^s(c_s))\,ds$. Three consequences follow. First, the plain covariance is always an upper bound: $0\le Reg\le-Cov(c,\pi^s(c))$. Second, when the optimal decision rule is affine, as in unconstrained and equality-constrained (e.g., budget-constrained Markowitz) quadratic programs, regret equals exactly one half of the covariance. For purely linear objectives, an affine rule forces zero regret. Third, the ratio of regret to covariance lies in $[0,1]$ and is governed by the shape of the covariance profile along the path. The noise level at which this profile first becomes positive is a decision-stability margin that tightens the bound. The identity also holds scenario by scenario for any predicted cost, so it applies to linear and combinatorial programs with discontinuous decision rules. We give dimension-free concentration bounds and a central limit theorem for the plug-in estimator. Across 7 problem classes, 8 cost distributions, and the shortest-path benchmark of Elmachtoub and Grigas (2022) with $10^6$ draws per configuration, the identities hold to within quadrature error, and the covariance bound holds in every scenario.
item.dc:creator: Irene Aldridge

item.title: Personalized Pricing with Invalid Instrumental Variables: Identification, Estimation, and Policy Learning
item.description: arXiv:2302.12670v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Pricing based on individual customer characteristics is widely used to maximize sellers' revenues. We study how a firm can learn such a personalized pricing policy from historical transactions when unobserved factors affect both the prices it charged and the revenue it earned. Standard instrumental variable (IV) methods either focus on a discrete treatment space or require that the IV affect revenue only through price. This exclusion restriction is difficult to justify in pricing, where the most natural candidate IVs are price-setting levers that may also affect revenue directly. We propose PRINT (Personalized pRicing using Invalid iNsTrumental variables), a policy learning method for continuous prices that uses such candidate IVs. Relying on structural models of revenue and price, we show that the optimal pricing policy can be identified with invalid IV that shifts higher moments of historical prices, when the unobserved factors that drive customers' price sensitivity are separated from those used by the historical pricing rule. Based on this identification, which leads to conditional moment restrictions with generalized residual functions, we construct an adversarial min-max estimator that accommodates flexible machine learning models and establish regret bounds for the learned pricing policy. Simulation studies and an application to a U.S. online auto lender illustrate the method's performance. Our results give a principled way to learn personalized prices from observational data using imperfect price-setting levers, and clarify when doing so is justified.
item.dc:creator: Rui Miao, Zhengling Qi, Cong Shi, Lin Lin

item.title: Online Multivariate Regularized Distributional Regression for High-dimensional Probabilistic Electricity Price Forecasting
item.description: arXiv:2504.02518v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Probabilistic electricity price forecasting (PEPF) is vital for short-term electricity markets, yet the multivariate nature of day-ahead prices - spanning 24 consecutive hours - remains underexplored. At the same time, real-time decision-making requires methods that are both accurate and fast. We introduce an online algorithm for multivariate distributional regression models, allowing efficient modeling of the conditional means, variances, and dependence structures of electricity prices. The approach combines multivariate distributional regression with online coordinate descent and LASSO-type regularization (absolute shrinkage and selection operator), enabling scalable estimation in high-dimensional covariate spaces. Additionally, we propose a regularized estimation path over increasingly complex dependence structures, allowing for early stopping and avoiding overfitting. In a case study using historical data from the German day-ahead market, the proposed method yields interpretable and well-calibrated joint prediction intervals for the 24-dimensional price distribution and provides robust performance across a range of proper scoring rules. The results underscore the importance of modeling the dependence structure of electricity prices. Furthermore, we analyze the trade-off between predictive accuracy and computational costs for batch and online estimation and provide a high-performing open-source Python implementation in the ondil package.
item.dc:creator: Simon Hirsch

item.title: Covariate-Adjusted Deep Causal Learning for Heterogeneous Panel Data Models
item.description: arXiv:2505.20536v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This paper studies the task of estimating heterogeneous treatment effects in causal panel data models with covariate effects. We propose a novel Covariate-Adjusted Deep Causal Learning (CoDEAL) framework that cohesively deals with the underlying heterogeneity and nonlinearity of both panel units and covariate effects. CoDEAL integrates nonlinear covariate effect components (parameterized by a feed-forward neural network) with nonlinear factor structures (modeled by a multi-output autoencoder) to form a heterogeneous causal panel model. The nonlinear covariate component flexibly captures complex covariate influences on outcomes, and the nonlinear factor decomposition enables CoDEAL to effectively capture both cross-sectional and temporal dependencies inherent in the data panel. This latent structural information is subsequently integrated into a customized matrix completion algorithm, thereby facilitating more accurate counterfactual imputation. Moreover, the use of a multi-output autoencoder explicitly accounts for heterogeneity across units and enhances the model interpretability of the latent factors. We establish theoretical guarantees on the convergence of the estimated counterfactuals and demonstrate the compelling performance of the proposed method using extensive simulation studies and real-world data applications.
item.dc:creator: Guanhao Zhou, Yuefeng Han, Xiufan Yu

item.title: Comparative e-backtesting
item.description: arXiv:2511.05840v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Backtesting risk measures is a central task in financial regulation. While traditional backtests evaluate whether a forecasting model is statistically consistent with observed losses, regulatory practice often requires assessing the performance of an internal model relative to standard models. In this paper, we develop a parametric anytime-valid framework for comparative backtests of general risk measures using e-values and e-processes. We construct likelihood-based e-processes for comparative e-backtests with validity and power guarantees. As practical guidelines, we propose the e-three-zone approach based on weak dominance, and introduce the overall and resetting test schemes for different practical purposes. Simulation studies and empirical analyses are conducted to show practical manipulations in financial regulation.
item.dc:creator: Zhanyi Jiao, Qiuqi Wang, Yimiao Zhao

item.title: Causal Multi-Task Demand Learning
item.description: arXiv:2602.09969v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study multi-task demand learning for retail pricing, where firms seek to estimate heterogeneous linear price-response functions across many decision contexts. Each context has rich covariates but limited price variation, motivating transfer across tasks. However, such transfer is complicated by endogeneity: prices may be arbitrarily correlated with unobserved task-level demand determinants. We propose a meta-learning framework that identifies the conditional mean of task-specific causal demand parameters despite this confounding, provided each task contains at least two distinct, locally exogenous price points. The key is to carefully design the information available to the learner. We condition on the full price history to address cross-task confounding, but withhold the demand outcomes associated with two locally exogenous price points to preserve identifiability. These withheld outcomes provide supervision through a randomized query. We establish that this information design is maximally uniformly valid for the squared-loss objective: any refinement of the conditioning set that reveals information about the withheld outcomes or the query index admits a data-generating process under which the objective no longer identifies the conditional mean causal target. Synthetic experiments demonstrate improved estimation of causal demand parameters under strong confounding, while retail experiments show improved held-out demand prediction relative to standard transfer-learning baselines.
item.dc:creator: Varun Gupta, Vijay Kamble

item.title: Conventional Inference under Nonstationary Heavy Tailed Fractional Processes & Arrays
item.description: arXiv:2610.25237v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Existing regression inference methods for nonstationary heavy tailed data are largely limited to unit roots tests. Functional central limit theorems (FCLTs), which are commonly used for the asymptotic analysis of nonstationary models, are inapplicable to nonstationary data characterized by a memory parameter $d<1$ and a stability parameter $\alpha<2$. Furthermore, it is well known that inference under nonstationarity is often non-conventional, and this issue is exacerbated in the presence of heavy-tailed data. The interaction of long memory and heavy tails significantly enlarges the nonstationary region---i.e., the covariate model space---where conventional inference methods typically fail. To address these challenges, we propose a new limit theory and methods that facilitate both workable asymptotics and conventional inference in parametric regressions involving stationary and nonstationary heavy-tailed covariate processes. Specifically, our approach develops a limit theory for three classes of heavy-tailed weakly nonstationary processes (hereafter, HT-WNPs), which lie on the threshold of nonstationarity (cf. Duffy and Kasparis, 2021, Annals of Statistics). We also develop limit theory for functionals of strongly nonstationary heavy-tailed fractional processes. We demonstrate that the proposed methods, particularly a weighted extension of IVX, facilitate conventional inference for a broad class of stationary and nonstationary heavy-tailed covariates. This class includes mildly and nearly integrated arrays, as well as nonstationary fractional processes with memory parameter $1-1/\alpha<d<2-1/\alpha$, where $\alpha\in(1,2]$. A related weighted instrumental-variable estimator is also considered, primarily for estimation purposes.
item.dc:creator: Ioannis Kasparis (University of Cyprus)
